records.title: LEAVE OUR HILLS ALONE!
records.bodyText:
Beautiful footage of the UNESCO Biosphere in Dumfries and Galloway
A great short movie showcasing the natural treasure that is in our landscapes, all of which are found in the hills surrounding Moniaive too, the village a designated Biosphere Community within the Galloway and Southern Ayrshire UNESCO Biosphere.
With climate resilience being a major concern, shouldn't every effort be made to protect the carbon absorbing peat, to plant native woodland, maintain sphagnum moss, protect our natural springs, streams and rivers and ensure that our hills absorb, slow down and prevent heavy downpours from once again flooding our homes?
https://youtu.be/lYad9S9TlTM?si=Uh_e_FG8_4QqX6Q_

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Where was the first grid connected wind turbine generator ?
Costa Head Wind Turbine Generator, Orkney.
Ernest William Golding was initially interested in the application of electricity to develop agricultural and horticultural processes. In 1945 he was appointed to the Electricity Research Association (ERA) as Head of the Rural Electrification department. Three years later in 1948 the ERA added wind power to his job description as Technical Secretary of the Wind Power Committee.
In 1948, preliminary work started in Orkney recording wind speeds at Costa Head, Vestra Fiold and other selected places including Grimsetter (now Kirkwall airport) and Bignold Park, Kirkwall. The research was supervised by the ERA for the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board, using local recorders as part of a project to develop wind generated electricity in the islands.
The ERA decided that Costa Hill would be the best site for their wind driven electric generator and in 1949 they placed an order with John Brown Ltd, the Clyde shipbuilders, for a turbine with 60 feet blades. The turbine used technology from both the
aircraft and marine sectors.
The 100 KW turbine had helicopter type blades and was erected on top of an 80 ft steel framework structure. Importantly it able to run unattended and in 1955 it connected up to the main Grid. This was seen as a back up to the oil fired power station in Kirkwall which would allow it to save on fuel.
1952 was the year of The Great Gale which hit Orkney and blew away thousands of hens as well as causing other extensive damage to the islands infrastructure. At Costa Hill wooden sheds
 were blown away and the 125 m.p.h. wind speeds broke the recording device. The steel skeletal structure had withstood the force of the winds.
Although the Hydro Board and the ERA were running the project, locally a farmer, Bill Sabiston, was managing the day to day workings of the wind turbine and the measurements of the other instruments located on the site. He is said to have worked 'under conditions which would terrify most people.' Bill Sabiston had been sceptical at first over whether the windmill would stand the force of winds in Orkney. 
There was interest from all over the UK, Ireland and across the world. 70 sites had been identified in the UK for the location of wind turbines, mainly in areas where other forms of generating electricity was not an option.
During the year 1957 all interest in the Costa Wind project disappears from newspapers. In the short space of two years the media, politicians and the public are no longer commenting on wind power or imagining the great benefits it could bring with cheaper electricity for hard to reach areas.
The Costa Hill turbine had ceased to function, but there were still working wind turbines in other
wind turbines in other countries.
Two events happened to change public, political and commercial interest in wind driven electricity: the opening of the oil fuelled Power Station in Kirkwall; and the building of a nuclear power station across the Pentland Firth at Dounreay in Caithness.
Critics of wind power often ask where the electricity is going to come from when the wind stops blowing – an issue deemed almost irrelevant at Costa Head, on account of winds in excess of 125mph and ‘the comparative absence of calm days’. The generation target of 100kW was to be achieved with a wind speed of 30mph or above.
This meant a blade circle of 60ft diameter, but later the ‘rated wind velocity’ was increased to 35mph, allowing the blade circle diameter to be decreased to 50ft.
In common with the machines that followed, the Costa Head wind turbine was built for completely automatic operation, so that it is possible to leave it entirely unattended for long periods. It consisted of a three-bladed propeller and nacelle mounted on top of a seven-ton steel tower 78ft above the ground. By means of a step-up gearbox, the hub speed of 130rpm could be increased to 750rpm for driving the electric generator. Yawing of the nacelle was obtained by mounting it on a pintle shaft and turning it with a bull ring and pinion driven at reduced speed by an electric motor.
Unlike today’s glass and carbon fibre composite blades, the three blades for Costa Head consisted of a compressed laminated wood spar fitted with spruce ribs, which were covered by 3/32in mahogany plywood skin and protected with plastic.
Inside each arm are fixed and moving pistons for varying the pitch of the blades, this was done hydraulically under the control of a servo-governor, the motion being transmitted through torque tubes and Hardy-Spicer couplings to quadrant boxes situated at the ends of the hub arms. Each blade root was attached by a quick-release fork to a universal joint, allowing the blade to ‘cone’ and ‘drag’ at speed, which helped avoid excessive bending stresses at the roots.
When the blade is at rest, this joint is automatically locked so as to hold the blade fixed. The movement of the blades on their hinges is controlled by hydraulic dampers in order to prevent excessive vibration.
A small ‘pilot’ windmill mounted on top of the nacelle controlled the starting and stopping of the windmill. To prevent the turbine being started by a sudden gust of wind, the pilot windmill averaged the wind speed over a number of minutes.  
Text by Fiona Morag Grahame.— in Orkney Islands.

records.title: Dunbar Against Massive Datacentres (DAMD)
records.bodyText:
Save the wildlife!
A few videos of some of the wildlife that have been seen in and adjacent to the fields of the proposed hyperscale AI datacentre development at Dunbar. There is so much more!! 47 species of birds, 15 species of butterflies and 12 species of mammals counted since last year. We need to keep these fields for nature!! 
A massive 60.2 hectares of wildlife habitat, currently grade 2 agricultural land, which is the size of 84 full sized football pitches, stretching from Asda to West Barns, a fifth of Dunbar.
Large flocks of pink footed geese in winter, swallows and house martins congregate at the start and end of summer, foxes and badgers to name a few .... see our 'albums' section for more photos of the wonderful wildlife seen.
Please record any wildlife records that you see in the fields in the proposed development area (see map in comments) and add to the irecord app as this is the way the records get submitted to the council to refer to when the planning application goes in. App | iRecord https://share.google/PU5HJjP9DQ2ePEMHq
Find out more about local concerns here:
https://sustainingdunbar.org/2026/11/data-centre-concerns/
Show the Scottish Government, East Lothian Council and Ken Ross and his company Thistle Sands Ltd that we don't want this.
Join more than 80 organisations on the march on Saturday down the Royal Mile in Edinburgh on Saturday 14th November.
https://fb.me/e/lvZVqPzCH
Please sign our local petition if you haven't already:

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
A delay to a planned wind farm in Bronte Country could spell the end of the project, campaigners have said.
Developer Calderdale Wind Farm Limited (CWFL) planned to build 34 turbines on Walshaw Moor, between Hebden Bridge and Haworth, but was forced to pause after consultations identified "a number of matters requiring further consideration".
CWFL was due to submit a Development Consent Order application for Calderdale Energy Park this month, but has now delayed the application until July 2027. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjvg2rg6530ro

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
In the 1930s, Scotland's electricity network was split in two, with a unified 132kV National Grid system covering Central and Southern Scotland while the Highlands remained completely separate.
Following the Electricity (Supply) Act 1926 and the formation of the Central Electricity Board, a high-voltage 132kV transmission system was developed across Central and Southern Scotland.
By the late 1930s, the Scottish system was fully tied into the broader British National Grid, linking major steam, coal, and early hydro-electric generators (such as the Falls of Clyde and Rannoch power stations) to industrial and population centers.
Central Scotland Electricity Scheme
By 1927 the Central Scotland scheme was the first scheme proposed to the Central Electricity Board for linking up the national electricity network; it affected c.5000 sq.miles of central Scotland. 
Out of the existing 36 generating stations in the area, 10 would be retained, to be reduced eventually to 6, 2 of which would be extended (at Dalmarnock and Portobello) and 2 new ones built; a series of high voltage transmission lines would be constructed to link up the various undertakings; the frequency of the alternating current would be standardised at 50 Hertz.
The selected stations were:
Yoker Power Station
Port Dundas Generating Station
Clyde's Mill Power Station
Portobello Power Station
Dalmarnock Power Station
Stonebyres and Corra Linn (Bonnington) Power Stations
A further 4 stations would be retained temporarily:
Bonnybridge Power Station
Carolina Port Power Station
Dunfermline Power Station
Kilmarnock Power Station
As a result 132kv Grid Substations were constructed in the 1930s at each power station. 
The 132kV National Grid did not extend north of the Central Belt. A single transmission line owned by the Grampian Electricity Supply Company stretched up toward Rannoch, driven by early hydro developments.
Major proposals to build widespread hydroelectric schemes in the Highlands—such as the 1938 Caledonian Water Power Bill—were fiercely opposed by landowners, sporting estates, local councils (like Inverness County Council), and the coal mining industry, leading to their defeat in Parliament.
Because the national grid bypassed the highland region, the northern territory had to wait until the 1940s and the creation of the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board to develop its own distinct regional transmission network.
Very little of original 132Kv grid network remains but if you are driving north over the Kincardine Bridge, on your LHS are the four concrete foundations blocks that supported the 132Kv Forth Crossing towers. This was later superseded by the 500ft tall 275 Kv double circuit Forth Crossing in the 1960s.— at Kincardine Bridge.

records.title: Deeside Against Pylons
records.bodyText:
It’s only right that when local volunteers and landowners are left doing the applicant’s homework it deserves attention!
It demonstrates that something is very wrong and the process is broken if we have to do the legwork for an energy giant and its £30 billion project! 
John Campbell, NOTKUP Project Manager, put the Reporters on notice at the end of the last PLI Hearing that we (Deeside Against Pylons, Stop Tealing Industrialisation Group and APAG) along with Galbraith would be seeking expenses from SSEN, arguing that volunteers and landowners were left to expose errors and inaccuracies, fill gaps and challenge omissions at their own cost.
They will put their recommendation to Scottish Ministers as to whether our claim against SSEN’s unreasonable behaviour is justified.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
𝐍𝐄𝐒𝐎'𝐒 𝐄𝐋𝐄𝐂𝐓𝐑𝐈𝐂𝐈𝐓𝐘 𝐌𝐀𝐑𝐆𝐈𝐍 𝐖𝐀𝐑𝐍𝐈𝐍𝐆 – 𝐖𝐀𝐒 𝐈𝐓 𝐋𝐎𝐎𝐊𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐀𝐓 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐖𝐑𝐎𝐍𝐆 𝐓𝐇𝐈𝐍𝐆?
On Sunday evening, 8 November, NESO issued an Electricity Margin Notice (EMN), warning that electricity supplies could be tight between 6am and 11am on Monday.
But there was something odd about this warning. Monday evening was actually expected to be considerably tighter than the morning, yet NESO issued no warning for the evening.
Kathryn Porter has examined the available data and believes the way NESO accounts for battery storage may help explain what happened.
In simple terms:
Britain now has around 8.7 GW of battery storage. These batteries can provide substantial amounts of electricity, but only for limited periods before they need recharging.
On Monday morning, batteries were initially discharging electricity, but their scheduled output then dropped dramatically. Many were effectively taken out of the picture.
Battery operators had a commercial incentive to save their stored electricity for the evening, when electricity prices were much higher.
Yet broadly the same battery capacity was physically available during both the morning and evening peaks.
By relying on commercial schedules rather than properly assessing the batteries' actual capabilities, NESO may have underestimated the capacity available in the morning and overestimated what would be available in the evening.
The consequences could be significant.
NESO was paying extraordinarily high prices to secure additional electricity capacity, while potentially failing to make the best use of battery storage already available.
It also raises questions about why NESO did not make better use of the Balancing Mechanism to call on available battery capacity.
The underlying problem appears to be that NESO has invested in a system increasingly dependent on battery flexibility, but its operational systems may not yet be capable of properly managing that flexibility.
Kathryn points out that NESO has already recognised deficiencies in its battery modelling and introduced new requirements for battery operators to provide information about how long they can sustain their output.
But having the information is not the same as being able to use it effectively.
The question is whether NESO's control-room systems are keeping pace with the increasingly complex electricity system it is supposed to manage.
And, perhaps most importantly, given the ludicrously high costs paid to gas plants on Monday,  whether consumers are paying for expensive additional capacity when existing resources are not being used as effectively as they could be.
What we ask - and, again, this is something which Kathryn Porter has highlighted previously - how can NESO  manage an increasingly complex electricity system, dependent on real-time balancing of intermittent generation, imports, storage and conventional generation, if its underlying operational processes and systems are still reliant on manual intervention and are struggling to model the capabilities of the very technologies being introduced to support that system?
https://watt-logic.com/.../nesos-latest-emn-made-little.../
